Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 220 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2020) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit 220 (WMU 220), Red Deer, covers an area of 2,672 km 2. The WMU contains the City of 
Red Deer, which was not surveyed, but is known to have populations of mule deer, white -tailed deer, and moose in 
addition to those reported here. The Red Deer river winds its way through the north-central portion of the WMU, 
and  headwaters of Ghostpine, Haynes, Kneehill, Spruce, and Three Hills Creeks occur. Pine Lake is the largest 
waterbody, and the Pine Lake Morraine is a significant feature of the WMU. Th e entire WMU falls within the central 
parkland. The WMU is primarily deeded land, with limited Crown parcels, and has significant agriculture and 
acreage development. There are remaining large tracts of forest in the Red Deer River Valley and associated 
drainages, as well as the south central portion of the WMU. 
 
A survey for ungulates (mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose) was last conducted for WMU 220 in 2003 using 
the random stratified block methodology (Random Block). See Table 1 for previous ungula te survey estimates for 
WMU 220. 
 
The objective of the December 2019 survey was to assess the status of the ungulate population in WMU 220 by 
determining estimates for abundance, density and age-sex composition. We also recorded observations of 
additional species of game management or conservation concern including carnivores, game birds,  and sensitive 
or At Risk species. 
 
Survey method 
The transect survey was conducted flying 40 north-south lines at 1.6 km intervals, with 25% coverage (400 m wide 
survey strip) from Dec 16-19, 2019 for a total linear survey effort of 1,605 km. At each observation point, ungulates 
were classified by species, and when possible, sex and age were recorded. Antler size for deer was classified as 
‘small’ (spike or two points on one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more points; antlers inside ears) or 
large (antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of ears). 
 
Density was  calculated for white-tailed deer, mule deer and moose following Jolly 1969 (as described in Krebs  
2014) for surveys conducted with unequal sized units without replacement because the transect lengths varied. 
Density was multiplied by the WMU area to determine population estimates. 90% confidence intervals were also 
calculated. 
 
Elk observations were recorded during the survey, but population estimates were not calculated because the 
design of this survey is not appropriate for elk population calculation. 
 
Results 
A total of 695 white-tailed deer were observed in 191 groups. The estimated density was 1.08 deer/km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 2,897 individuals (90% CI 2,422 – 3,372). A total of 695 white-tailed deer were 
classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 16:100:67. That results in an estimated 2020 early 
winter white-tailed deer population of 253 buck, 1,593 doe, and 1,072 fawn. Of the 60 white-tailed deer bucks 
classified, 42% were classified ‘small’, 40% ‘medium’, and 18% ‘large’. 
 
A total of 535 mule deer were observed in 130 groups. The estimated density was 0.83 mule deer/km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 2,227 individuals (90% CI 1,808 – 2,646). A total of 509 mule deer were classified and

the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 40:100:65. That results in an estimated 2020 early winter mule deer 
population of  434 buck, 1,087 doe, and 706 fawn. Of the 99 mule deer bucks classified, 28% were ‘small’, 42%  
‘medium’, and 33% ‘large’. 
 
A total of 129 moose were observed in 66 groups. The estimated density was 0.20 moose/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 537 individuals (90% CI 470 – 604). A total of 121 moose were classified and the bull:cow:calf 
ratio was estimated to be 53:100:67. That results in an estimated 2020 early winter moose population of 129 bull, 
244 cow, and 164 calf. 
 
One group of 13 elk was observed during the survey (one bull, seven cows, five calves).  
 
We also observed 87 coyotes, 28 grey partridge, 11 bald eagle, one great horned owl, and one snowy owl.  These 
are incidental observations only and should not be considered minimum total counts.
